1.title: Documentation and Lifecycle Management
1.text: Welcome to Module sixteen: Documentation and Lifecycle Management. This module covers documentation and lifecycle management. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do four things. What to document for a Claude solution. How to give implementation guidance to a delivery team. The lifecycle phases and the architect's role in each. Change management for models, prompts and data.

1.title: Case Check-In: Lumen Advisory Hands Over a Claims Assistant to the Insurer's Team
1.text: Our running case is Lumen Advisory. Lumen Advisory Hands Over a Claims Assistant to the Insurer's Team. Lumen's engagement ends in three months; the insurer's team must run, monitor and evolve the system. Two prior projects failed to survive hand-off because prompts lived in a developer's notebook.

1.title: Documenting an Architecture
1.text: Documenting an Architecture. The figure shows this: A documentation set: context and goals, architecture and data flow, decision records, interfaces and prompts, evaluation and operations, runbooks and handoff.

1.title: Documenting an Architecture, continued
1.text: Documenting an Architecture, continued. Context and goals. Problem, users, success criteria, constraints, non-goals. Architecture overview. Components, pattern, data flow, trust boundaries, platform and region. Decision records (A D R s). Decision, options, trade-offs, date, owner, status. Interfaces. A P I (application programming interface) and tool schemas, M C P (Model Context Protocol) servers, authentication, error handling. Prompts and configuration. Versioned system prompts, templates, model I Ds and parameters, retrieval settings, Skills, Claude dot M D. Data. Sources, ownership, chunking and index design, refresh schedule, retention, access rules. Evaluation. Datasets, metrics, thresholds, how to run the eval suite, results history. Security and compliance. Threat model, controls, regime mapping, D P A s and B A A s, audit evidence.

1.title: Documenting an Architecture, continued
1.text: Documenting an Architecture, continued. Operations. Dashboards, alerts, S L O s, runbooks, incident process, on-call, cost budgets. Handoff. Known issues, backlog, upgrade path, contacts. Docs live with the code: in the repository, reviewed with changes; keep prompts, schemas and evals in version control. Use diagrams (context, components, sequence for key flows, data flow) and keep them current. Write for the reader's task: onboarding, changing a prompt, responding to an alert. Do not store secrets in docs; point to the secrets manager. Exam tip: A complete handoff includes versioned prompts and configuration, evals, runbooks and decision records, not only code and a diagram.

1.title: Implementation Guidance
1.text: Implementation Guidance. Give delivery teams clear guidelines: patterns to use and to avoid, prompt and tool conventions, error-handling and retry policy, logging standards, security rules, evaluation gates, naming and versioning. Provide a reference implementation or template repository. Define a definition of done: eval thresholds met, security review complete, runbook written, monitoring in place. Set up reviews: architecture review for significant changes; prompt and eval review for behavior changes. Start thin: a vertical slice (one workflow end to end with eval and monitoring) before widening. Capture coding-assistant conventions for the team (Claude dot M D, shared settings, Skills) so A I-assisted development follows standards (Module seventeen).

1.title: Lifecycle Phases
1.text: Lifecycle Phases. The figure shows this: The lifecycle: discovery, design, build and test, handoff and launch, then monitor and iterate in a loop.

1.title: Lifecycle Phases, continued
1.text: Lifecycle Phases, continued. Discovery. Architect's focus: Requirements, constraints, data, risk, success criteria. Outputs: Problem statement, risks, baselines (Modules one and fifteen). Design. Architect's focus: Pattern, model, retrieval, integration, security, compliance, evaluation plan. Outputs: Architecture, A D R s, threat model. Build and test. Architect's focus: Prototype, vertical slice, evals, security tests, load tests. Outputs: Working system, eval results. Handoff and launch. Architect's focus: Documentation, training, runbooks, staged rollout, S L A s (service level agreement). Outputs: Handoff pack, canary plan. Monitor and iterate. Architect's focus: Dashboards, quality sampling, feedback loop, cost control, change management. Outputs: Improvement backlog, reports. Retire or migrate. Architect's focus: Model and platform retirements, data deletion. Outputs: Migration plan.

1.title: Change Management for Models, Prompts and Data
1.text: Change Management for Models, Prompts and Data. Model version upgrade or retirement. Risk: Behavior and prompts shift; old models retire (Anthropic-operated platforms commit to dates; partner platforms set their own). Practice: Pin I Ds; track retirement dates; run regression evals on the new model; migrate by canary; update prompts per the model's guidance. Prompt changes. Risk: Silent quality shifts. Practice: Version, review, A or B test, roll back. Data and index refresh. Risk: Stale or broken retrieval. Practice: Validate after each refresh; monitor index age. Tool or A P I changes. Risk: Breaking schemas. Practice: Contract tests; versioned tools; deprecation notices. Regulatory change. Risk: New obligations. Practice: Compliance review calendar.

1.title: Change Management for Models, Prompts and Data, continued
1.text: Change Management for Models, Prompts and Data, continued. Scale growth. Risk: Rate limits, cost. Practice: Capacity plan, tiers, batch, caching. Keep an upgrade playbook: evaluate, adjust, canary, monitor, retire the old path. Own the backlog: tech debt in prompts, evals and docs is real debt. Plan knowledge transfer: who owns prompts, knowledge bases, evals and on-call after the architect leaves. Exam tip: Prompts, schemas and evals are code: version them and review them with the change. Exam tip: Plan model retirements early: pin, run regression evals, canary, then retire the old path.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. Docs: Context, architecture, A D R s, interfaces, prompts and config, data, evals, security, operations, handoff. Store: With the code, versioned and reviewed; no secrets. Guidance: Patterns, conventions, reference implementation, definition of done, reviews. Phases: Discovery, design, build and test, handoff and launch, monitor and iterate, retire or migrate. Changes: Pin models; regression evals; canary; prompt versioning; data validation; contract tests. Ownership: Named owners; knowledge transfer.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. The architect's engagement ends soon. Which handoff package best lets the client's team operate the system? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Operations need prompts, evals, runbooks and reasoning, not just code.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. A prompt change shipped last month cannot be traced. What practice would have prevented this? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Prompts are code, so keeping them in version control with review, tests and release notes makes every change traceable.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. A model used in production will be retired on a published date. What is the best approach? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Plan migrations early with evals and a gradual rollout.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. Select two. Which two belong in a definition of done for a new Claude feature? The five options are on the screen. The answers are A and B. Quality gates and operational readiness make a feature done.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. What is the best way to begin building a large Claude solution? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. A slice proves the architecture and exposes risk early.

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. Where should architecture documents and prompts be stored? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Docs and prompts evolve with the system and need review.

1.title: Practice Question 7
1.text: Question seven. Which lifecycle phase includes quality sampling, dashboards and the improvement backlog? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Monitor and iterate is the ongoing operation phase, where quality sampling and dashboards feed the improvement backlog.

1.title: Practice Question 8
1.text: Question eight. A tool provider changes a response schema and the agent breaks. Which practice reduces such breakage? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Contract tests and versioned tool schemas with deprecation notices catch breaking changes before they reach production.

1.title: Practice Question 9
1.text: Question nine. Who should own prompts, knowledge bases and evals after the architect leaves? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Ownership and knowledge transfer keep the system healthy.

1.title: Practice Question 10
1.text: Question ten. Which document records why a vector database was chosen over keyword search alone? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. An architecture decision record documents the options considered and the trade-offs behind a choice such as a vector database.

1.title: Answers at a Glance
1.text: Here are all ten answers. Question one: C. Question two: D. Question three: C. Question four: A and B. Question five: C. Question six: D. Question seven: D. Question eight: A. Question nine: A. Question ten: B. In the next module, we continue the course.
